title: Nvidia Halts AI Server Shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia
yt_title: Nvidia STOPS AI Server Shipments to 4 Asian Countries – Here's Why
yt_description:
Nvidia has told its partners to stop shipping AI servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to the Financial Times. Dell and Supermicro told customers there that Nvidia won't authorize their orders, after a new US export rule gave regional cloud providers 90 days to get a licence and prove none of their users face US restrictions. The target: Chinese AI developers renting Nvidia chips from cloud providers in Southeast Asia. Here's what changed, why the region matters ($104 billion through Nvidia's Singapore unit in 2025) and what happens next.

script: Welcome to IT News, AI News! Breaking today: Nvidia just hit the pause button on a whole region. According to the Financial Times, Nvidia told its partners to stop shipping AI servers to four Southeast Asian countries. Those are Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia. Four countries, zero new Nvidia AI servers. For now. Server makers Dell and Supermicro told customers there that Nvidia will not authorize their orders. So why the sudden stop? Blame a new United States export rule that came into effect last week. Here's the loophole it targets. Chinese AI developers could not buy top Nvidia chips, so they rented them instead, from cloud providers in these countries. Under the new rule, those cloud providers have ninety days to get a license from the US Commerce Department. To get it, they must prove that none of their end users face US export restrictions. That's a lot of paperwork, even for a robot. One cloud executive told the Financial Times: there's a new rule, but no guidance on how to carry it out. And the money here is huge. Nvidia booked one hundred and four billion dollars of revenue through its Singapore unit in twenty twenty-five, up seventy-two percent. Part of that also covers Taiwan and China, but it shows how big this hub has become. The pressure has been building. On November sixteenth, US officials confirmed a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, a Singapore cloud company suspected of funnelling Nvidia chips to China. And it lands just days after Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia's boss. Some hoped that meant softer enforcement. So far, no sign of that. Is the pause temporary? Nobody knows yet. Nvidia and its partners are still working out how to comply. Nvidia, Dell and Supermicro did not immediately comment. One thing is clear: the AI chip race now runs through the paperwork office.
